newsitem.title: USA: Wife of gun victim Brady disappointed by ruling.
newsitem.headline: Wife of gun victim Brady disappointed by ruling.

text.p: Sarah Brady, whose husband was wounded in an assassination attempt on President Ronald Reagan, said background checks on handgun buyers were likely to continue despite Friday's Supreme Court ruling on the Brady gun control law.
A bitterly divided Supreme Court stuck down as unconstitutional a key provision of the Brady gun control law that required local sheriffs to conduct background checks on prospective handgun buyers.

At a news conference on the court's steps, Brady said she was disappointed by the ruling but pleased that the justices left intact another key provision that requires a five-day waiting period for purchasing a gun.

"The court's decision means that local law enforcement officials in 23 states are no longer required by federal law to do background checks on prospective handgun purchasers during the waiting period," Brady said. "It does not mean those checks will not occur."
"The Brady law was not gutted today," she told reporters.
She said the court's decision was not a victory for the National Rifle Association (NRA), which opposed the law. The NRA had supported the background checks, but opposed the waiting period.
"They got just the opposite today," she added. "They got a waiting period with no background check."
She has been a tireless crusader for gun control laws since her husband James Brady was shot in the head in 1981 by gunman John Hinkley, who tried to kill Reagan.
James Brady, who was serving as Reagan's press secretary at the time of the shooting, has been bound to a wheelchair ever since.
Sarah Brady told reporters that she informed her husband of the Supreme Court decision after he woke up from several hours of surgery at a local hospital.
"He gave a weak thumbs up," she said.
